strengths: Introduces a novel concept-based adversarial attack framework that generalizes single-image attacks by operating on an entire concept represented as a set of images or a probabilistic generative model.

Provides a probabilistic formalization linking concept-based attacks to traditional adversarial attacks, with two theoretical results that offer intuition and a tractable estimator for comparing KL divergences.

Extensive experiments across multiple classifiers (ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ViT-Base in the appendix), baselines (NCF, ACA, DiffAttack, ProbAttack), and metrics (white-box success, transferability, CLIP similarity, user study, no-reference image quality).

Strong empirical results: the proposed method achieves 97.82% white-box targeted attack success on ResNet50, outperforming DiffAttack (84.23%) and ProbAttack (59.23%), while also improving concept-preservation and image-quality metrics.
Proposes practical concept augmentation using SDXL LoRA and GPT-4o prompts, and introduces conservative/aggressive sample-selection strategies with a sensitivity study.
Clear writing, helpful figures, discussion of limitations, broader impacts, and reproducibility details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Theoretical assumptions are strong and may not reflect practical diffusion-based distributions: p_dis is assumed Gaussian with identical mean between single-image and concept distributions, while actual diffusion likelihoods are complex and non-Gaussian.

Empirical KL validation is not statistically convincing for several concepts: Table 3 reports large standard deviations, and for multiple concepts (e.g., poop_emoji, wolf_plushie, rc_car, shiny_sneaker) the mean is smaller than the standard deviation, so the claim that Δ<0 for every concept is not statistically supported.

Black-box transferability is reported only at top-100, not top-1; top-1 transfer is uniformly low, so the practical targeted transfer threat is limited, and top-100 success may overstate the attack’s effectiveness.

The core sampling procedure from the adversarial distribution p_adv ∝ p_vic p_dis is not described in sufficient detail in the main text. It is unclear whether classifier guidance, Langevin dynamics, or rejection sampling is used, which hurts reproducibility.
The method is computationally expensive: roughly 8 hours of diffusion fine-tuning per concept plus SDXL LoRA training, making the approach resource-intensive and limiting practical reproducibility.
Evaluation is limited to the DreamBoothPlus dataset with 26 concepts and 30 randomly selected target classes; broader concept diversity and larger-scale validation are missing.
The user study uses only five annotators and does not report inter-annotator agreement, and CLIP similarity can be an imperfect proxy for human concept preservation.

strengths: The paper proposes a conceptually interesting extension of adversarial attacks from single images to a whole concept represented by a set of images or a probabilistic generative model.
It builds on a probabilistic adversarial attack framework and attempts to connect traditional and concept-level attacks through KL divergence analysis.
The use of modern generative models (SDXL, LoRA, GPT-4o prompts) to augment DreamBooth concepts into DreamBoothPlus is practical and creates more diverse concept datasets.
The experimental evaluation covers multiple ImageNet classifiers, including adversarial-defense models, and reports both attack success and image-quality/similarity metrics.
The aggressive sample-selection strategy achieves high white-box targeted success and improved transferability on several models, and the paper includes a user study and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited relative to prior work. Song et al. (2018) already constructed unrestricted adversarial examples using generative models for class-level concepts, and Zhang et al. (2024) provides the probabilistic attack framework. The paper does not experimentally compare against the closest prior concept/class-level generative attack.

The theoretical contribution is weak. Theorem 1 only states that KL divergence to a Gaussian decreases with variance under a condition; it does not prove that concept-based attacks improve attack success or transferability. Theorem 2 is an algebraic identity, and the key claim Delta < 0 is only shown empirically on a small dataset.

The method for sampling from the adversarial distribution p_adv is not clearly specified. The paper fine-tunes a diffusion model to fit p_dis and then generates/selects samples using the classifier, which is closer to generate-and-test than principled sampling from p_vic * p_dis. Algorithmic details, guidance mechanism, and likelihood estimation are missing or relegated to vague appendix descriptions.

The comparison is not a fair threat model. The proposed method uses a 30-image concept set, per-concept generative fine-tuning (roughly 8 GPU-hours per concept), SDXL augmentation, and multiple samples, while baselines such as ACA, DiffAttack, and ProbAttack operate from a single image. This makes the claimed higher attack efficiency and success rate incomparable and unsupported.

The transferability results are weak and presented misleadingly. The paper reports top-100 targeted success rather than standard top-1; for 1000 ImageNet classes, top-100 has a 10% random chance. Many reported values are only modestly above chance, and the conservative variant often underperforms DiffAttack despite the text claiming comparable or better performance.

The similarity claim is contradicted by the CLIP scores. In Table 2, Ours (CONS) and Ours (AGGR) have lower average CLIP similarity than NCF and ProbAttack, and Ours (AGGR) is also slightly lower than DiffAttack, yet the text claims both strategies outperform other methods in similarity.

The user study is weak evidence for concept preservation. It uses only five annotators, with no inter-annotator agreement, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. Concept preservation is central to the paper but is not measured rigorously.

Important baselines and ablations are missing. There is no comparison to Song et al. (2018), no standard unrestricted attacks beyond color/latent methods, and no systematic ablation of concept size K, augmentation source, sample-selection budget M, target-class sensitivity, or the effect of using real versus generated concept images.

The practical cost is very high (hours of fine-tuning per concept), and the paper acknowledges being slower, which directly conflicts with claims of higher efficiency. Reproducibility is also limited because the promised code repository is not linked in the manuscript, and critical implementation details are absent.

The paper makes broad claims about the future of adversarial attacks and defense, but the empirical evidence is limited to 26 concepts and 30 target classes. The significance and generality of the contribution are therefore overstated.

strengths: Introduces a novel concept-based adversarial attack that extends the probabilistic adversarial attack framework from single images to entire concepts, a timely direction in generative-model-era security.
Provides theoretical analysis (Theorems 1–2) and an empirical KL-difference study that supports the intuition that concept-level distance distributions overlap more with victim distributions.
Proposes a practical concept augmentation pipeline using SDXL LoRA and GPT-4o to build diverse concept datasets.
Extensive experiments compare against strong unrestricted attacks (NCF, ACA, DiffAttack, ProbAttack), include white-box/transfer/defense classifiers, image-quality metrics, and a user study.

Achieves high white-box targeted attack success and improved transferability/image quality over DiffAttack and ProbAttack in many settings, e.g., 97.82% white-box and better top-100 transfer with AGGR.
Additional experiments with different surrogate models (MobileNetV2, ViT-Base) strengthen the empirical claims.
weaknesses: Theoretical support is not fully aligned with the empirical claim: Theorem 1 is univariate and concerns KL(p_vic||p_dis), while the empirical study estimates KL(p_dis||p_vic); the multivariate condition also omits the dimension factor, so the concept-level KL reduction is not rigorously established.
The central sampling procedure for p_adv ∝ p_vic p_dis with the fine-tuned diffusion model is not described in the main text or appendix; no algorithm box, making the core method hard to reproduce.
The KL-difference estimation relies on diffusion ELBO and an ad hoc p_share correction; the resulting large negative Δ estimates are not clearly linked to attack success or semantic overlap.

Missing comparison to generative unrestricted attack baselines such as Song et al. (2018) and to baselines given the same multi-image/concept-level capability; the improvement may partly stem from extra data and compute rather than the proposed formulation.
Transferability is reported only at top-100 because top-1 transfer is uniformly low; this weakens practical significance for realistic targeted attacks.
The method requires roughly 8 hours of H100 fine-tuning per concept, plus SDXL LoRA training, and no code URL is given in the manuscript, limiting reproducibility.
CLIP similarity is sometimes lower than ProbAttack/NCF despite high user-study scores, indicating tension in the concept-preservation evaluation metrics.

strengths: Introduces a concept-based adversarial attack framework that extends probabilistic adversarial attacks from a single image to an identity-level concept distribution, defining a new threat model.
Provides a probabilistic formulation and KL-divergence-based analysis, with an empirical Monte Carlo estimate of Δ, linking concept expansion to reduced distance from the victim distribution.
Develops a practical concept-augmentation pipeline using SDXL LoRA and GPT-4o prompts, plus conservative/aggressive sample-selection strategies.
Reports strong white-box targeted attack success rates and improved image-quality/similarity metrics compared with NCF, ACA, DiffAttack, and ProbAttack on DreamBoothPlus.
Includes extensive reproducibility details, hyperparameters, code/data descriptions, and an ethics/mitigation statement.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core mathematical extension is essentially replacing x_ori with C_ori in the prior ProbAttack formulation; Theorem 1 is basic calculus and Theorem 2 is a definitional KL identity.

Theoretical justification is incomplete: the condition in Theorem 1 may not hold for semantically close target classes, the mapping from concept distributions to decreased β is vague, and the Δ estimates have large variance and rely on an ad hoc likelihood-correction model.

Evaluation fairness is questionable: the proposed method uses a concept dataset and expensive per-concept fine-tuning (about 8 hours) while single-image baselines do not, and comparisons conflate the attack method with the quality of the underlying generative model.

Transferability remains very low (top-1 often <2%, top-5 often <12%) and is not consistently better than DiffAttack or ProbAttack, while the abstract’s claim of “higher attack efficiency” is misleading given the much slower runtime.

The user study uses only five annotators without significance tests, and CLIP similarity for the proposed method is lower than ProbAttack, weakening the claim that it better preserves the original concept.
Practical applicability is limited by the need to collect many concept images and fine-tune a diffusion model per concept, which the paper itself acknowledges as slower than comparable attacks.
Ethical presentation is concerning: concrete malicious use cases such as evading prohibited-item classifiers and adversarial patch T-shirts are described, though mitigation strategies are discussed.

strengths: Introduces and formalizes an identity-level concept-based adversarial attack, extending the probabilistic adversarial framework from a single image to a concept distribution.
Provides a broad empirical study on DreamBoothPlus with multiple classifiers, targeted/transfer settings, similarity metrics, image-quality metrics, a user study, and detailed appendices.
Reports strong white-box targeted attack success and generally better image quality/similarity than several unrestricted attack baselines.
Includes reproducibility and ethics statements, code availability claims, practical usage guidelines, and some mitigation discussion.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core method is essentially replacing x_ori with a concept distribution C_ori in the existing ProbAttack framework. The authors themselves describe it as a straightforward extension, and no fundamentally new attack mechanism or learning algorithm is introduced.

Theoretical support is weak. Theorem 1 is a generic Gibbs-distribution property whose key condition is assumed rather than proved for concept distributions. Theorem 2 is essentially the definition of the KL difference, not a substantive result. There is no rigorous proof that concept expansion reduces KL divergence or yields higher attack success in practice.

The empirical KL-difference evidence is unconvincing. Table 4 reports large standard deviations, with several concepts whose confidence intervals include zero (e.g., bear plushie, poop emoji, wolf plushie, shiny sneaker). This contradicts the claim that Δ<0 for every concept. The likelihood correction and common-random-number estimation are heuristic, and diffusion likelihoods are only approximate.

Evaluation is not compute-matched or threat-model matched. Baselines attack a single image, while the proposed method uses a concept dataset, generative augmentation via SDXL/LoRA/GPT-4o, roughly 8 hours of per-concept diffusion finetuning, classifier-guided sampling, and M-sample selection. The white-box gains may partly reflect additional data and compute rather than the concept-level idea itself.

Transferability is weak in absolute terms and not consistently better than DiffAttack. Top-5 transfer rates are often only around 1–11%, and the conservative strategy is sometimes worse than baselines. The paper's strong claims about improved attack efficiency and transferability are therefore overstated.

Concept-preservation evaluation is insufficient. The user study uses only five annotators, lacks inter-annotator agreement, and relies on a permissive 'same item' judgment. CLIP scores can be lower than ProbAttack despite claims of better preservation, and diversity is claimed but not quantitatively measured.

Practical significance and threat model are questionable. The method requires multiple identity images, costly per-concept generative finetuning, and white-box classifier access, making it less practical than standard adversarial attacks. The conclusion that this 'heralds the future of adversarial attacks' is overclaimed.

Positioning is incomplete: the paper does not experimentally compare against class-level unrestricted attacks or recent transferability-oriented unrestricted methods, and the main comparisons are against single-image perturbation attacks under different constraints.

strengths: Introduces a novel concept-based adversarial attack framework that extends probabilistic adversarial attacks from a single image to an entire concept distribution, enabling diverse and identity-preserving adversarial examples.
Provides theoretical analysis (Theorems 1 and 2) plus empirical KL-divergence estimates showing that the broader concept distribution reduces the divergence to the victim distribution.
Practical concept augmentation pipeline using SDXL/LoRA and GPT-4o prompts, with conservative and aggressive sample selection strategies.
Strong white-box targeted attack success (97.82% top-1 on ResNet50) and generally better image quality and user-study similarity than the compared baselines.
Good reproducibility: code, hyperparameters, compute resources, and ethical considerations are documented.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core change is replacing a single-image-centered distance distribution with a concept-centered one, while the theoretical results are relatively simple and do not fully justify the generality of the claims.

Evaluation lacks several recent unrestricted/class-level adversarial attack baselines (e.g., AdvDiff, NatADiff, AdvDiffuser, Song et al.), and the empirical study is limited to 26 concepts and 30 target classes.
Transferability remains modest: top-1 transfer rates are very low, and the main text reports top-5 success rates; this limits the practical impact of the claimed attack efficiency.
CLIP similarity scores are lower than ProbAttack and NCF, and the user study uses only five annotators without reporting agreement or statistical significance.

The threat model requires multiple concept images and expensive per-concept fine-tuning (about 8 hours per concept), which is a significant practical limitation compared with standard single-image attacks.
The theoretical condition E_p[D] > E_q[D] is asserted to always hold, but this is not rigorously established for arbitrary victim distributions and multimodal concept distributions.
